chapters.title: Counting people: rates, growth and the Lexis diagram
chapters.summary: Every population changes only through births, deaths and moves, and demographic rates divide those events by the person-years at risk. Growth compounds, so small rates produce large changes over a few generations. The Lexis diagram keeps track of age, period and cohort at once, and standardization and decomposition show how much of a difference between two populations is due to their age structure rather than their risks.

items.name: The demographic balancing equation
items.pic: A country as a tank with taps for births and immigration and drains for deaths and emigration; set the flows and the population counter obeys P(t+1) = P(t) + B − D + I − E exactly.

items.name: Person-years and occurrence–exposure rates
items.pic: Lifelines of individuals entering and leaving observation; the shaded total length is the person-years at risk, and deaths divided by that area give the rate.

items.name: Crude birth, death and growth rates
items.pic: Pick countries and years; the crude birth and death rates are drawn as two curves whose gap is the natural growth rate, with migration added as a separate band.

items.name: Growth rates, doubling times and the rule of 70
items.pic: Set an annual growth rate and see the population’s trajectory on linear and log axes; the doubling time read from the curve matches 70/r, and a 2% rate multiplies the population sevenfold in a century.

items.name: The Lexis diagram
items.pic: Lifelines run diagonally through a calendar-time × age grid; highlight a cohort, a period or an age group and the corresponding parallelogram, column or row lights up with its deaths counted.

items.name: The age–period–cohort identification problem
items.pic: Generate a death-rate surface from age, period and cohort effects you choose; then add any linear trend to the three effects in the way age = period − cohort allows and watch the fitted surface stay identical.

items.name: Direct and indirect age standardization
items.pic: Two populations with different age pyramids and death schedules; apply one standard population to both and see the crude ranking reverse when age composition is removed.

items.name: Simpson’s paradox in crude death rates
items.pic: A young country with higher death rates at every age has a lower crude death rate than an old country; drag the age structures and find where the paradox appears and disappears.

items.name: Kitagawa decomposition of a rate difference
items.pic: The difference between two crude rates is split into a rate effect and a composition effect, shown as stacked bars that always add up to the total difference.

items.name: Logistic forecasts of human population and their failure
items.pic: Fit a logistic curve to U.S. censuses up to 1920 as Pearl and Reed did; the fitted ceiling of about 200 million is drawn against the actual census counts that sailed past it.

chapters.title: The life table
chapters.summary: A life table follows a hypothetical cohort through a fixed schedule of death rates and summarizes it by survivorship, deaths, person-years and life expectancy. Life expectancy is simply the area under the survival curve, which is why infant deaths weigh so heavily on it. Multiple-decrement tables split deaths by cause and answer questions such as how much life expectancy would rise if a cause were eliminated.

items.name: Age-specific death rate mₓ and probability qₓ
items.pic: A one-year age group on the Lexis diagram: the rate divides deaths by person-years, the probability divides by people entering, and the two numbers diverge as mortality rises.

items.name: From rates to probabilities: the aₓ assumption
items.pic: Choose when within the interval deaths occur (aₓ); the conversion qₓ = nmₓ/(1 + (n − aₓ)mₓ) is drawn, and infant ages show why aₓ ≈ 0.1 matters.

items.name: Life-table columns: lₓ, dₓ, Lₓ, Tₓ, eₓ
items.pic: Edit a death schedule by dragging points; every life-table column is recomputed in a live table, with lₓ and dₓ plotted beside it.

items.name: Life expectancy is the area under the survival curve
items.pic: The survival curve l(x)/l(0) with its area shaded; the area equals the mean age at death computed from the dₓ histogram, and changing either picture changes both numbers identically.

items.name: Force of mortality (hazard) μ(x)
items.pic: Hazard drawn on a log scale beside the survival curve; drag the hazard and the survival curve bends, showing that survival falls fastest where the hazard is high.

items.name: Survival is the exponential of minus the cumulative hazard
items.pic: Shade the cumulative hazard up to age x; the readout exp(−area) matches l(x) from the life table, for any hazard curve you draw.

items.name: Period versus cohort life expectancy
items.pic: On a Lexis surface of improving mortality, the period table reads across a year while the cohort table follows a diagonal; the cohort figure comes out several years higher.

items.name: Surviving raises your life expectancy
items.pic: Plot x + eₓ against age: in a high-infant-mortality table life expectancy at age 5 exceeds that at birth, and the expected age at death keeps rising the longer you live.

items.name: Infant mortality dominates historical life expectancy
items.pic: Compare a 1750 and a 2020 life table: removing infant and child deaths alone closes most of the gap in e₀, shown as a decomposition by age.

items.name: Multiple-decrement life tables
items.pic: Stacked survival curves split deaths by cause; the area of each band is the expected years lost to each cause from birth.

items.name: Cause elimination and competing risks
items.pic: Remove a cause (cancer, heart disease) under the independence assumption; the new survival curve and the gain in e₀ are computed — often smaller than people guess, because other causes take over.

items.name: Healthy life expectancy (Sullivan method)
items.pic: Split each Lₓ by the prevalence of disability; the survival area divides into healthy and unhealthy years, and changing prevalence by age shows which ages drive the difference.

items.name: Lifespan inequality and Keyfitz’s entropy
items.pic: Two populations with the same e₀ but different spreads of age at death; the standard deviation and Keyfitz’s H are computed, and H also tells how much e₀ rises for a 1% cut in all death rates.

items.name: Observations upon the Bills of Mortality

paper.title: Natural and Political Observations Mentioned in a Following Index, and Made upon the Bills of Mortality
paper.venue: London: Tho. Roycroft for John Martin, James Allestry and Tho. Dicas

items.pic: Graunt’s London from the weekly bills: male christenings outnumber female by about 14 to 13, steadily year after year; and his table of survivors out of 100 born (64 at 6, 40 at 16, 25 at 26, 16 at 36, 10 at 46, 6 at 56, 3 at 66, 1 at 76, none at 86), drawn as the first survival curve and set against a modern London life table.

chapters.title: Patterns of mortality
chapters.summary: Adult death rates rise roughly exponentially with age, the regularity Gompertz found in 1825, with a constant added for age-independent deaths. Heterogeneity in frailty bends the curve at old ages, and whether mortality truly plateaus is debated. Model life tables and the Lee–Carter method summarize whole schedules with a few parameters, and the record life expectancy has risen with startling linearity for nearly two centuries.

items.name: Gompertz law of mortality
items.pic: Real adult death rates on a log scale fall near a straight line; fit the slope and read off the mortality-rate doubling time of about eight years.

items.name: Gompertz–Makeham law
items.pic: Add an age-independent Makeham term to the Gompertz line; it fits young-adult deaths and accidents, and its share of total mortality is shown by age.

items.name: Frailty: heterogeneity bends cohort hazards (Vaupel)
items.pic: A cohort mixes robust and frail individuals, each on a Gompertz curve; the frail die first, so the population hazard flattens at old ages even though no individual’s does.

items.name: Late-life mortality plateau (debated)
items.pic: Death rates above age 100 from validated data with their sparse-data error bars; toggle between a continuing Gompertz rise and a plateau and see which the intervals rule out.

items.name: Model life tables and the Brass logit system
items.pic: Two Brass parameters (level and shape) transform a standard survival curve; fit them to a country with sparse data and compare to its full table.

items.name: Lee–Carter mortality forecasting
items.pic: Decompose a log death-rate surface into an age pattern and a single time index by SVD; extrapolate the index as a random walk and draw the fan of forecast life expectancies.

items.name: Record life expectancy rises linearly (Oeppen–Vaupel)
items.pic: The highest national female e₀ each year since 1840 lies near a line of slope about three months per year; overlay past “maximum life expectancy” forecasts that were broken soon after.

items.name: Rectangularization of the survival curve
items.pic: Survival curves for successive decades become squarer as early deaths vanish; the age of steepest decline moves right and the lifespan variance shrinks.

items.name: Compression of morbidity (contested)
items.pic: Scenarios for healthy and unhealthy years as e₀ rises — compression, expansion or dynamic equilibrium — drawn as stacked survival areas next to observed trends.

items.name: The Preston curve
items.pic: Life expectancy against GDP per capita for countries in 1930, 1960 and 2020: the concave curve shifts upward over time, so at any income people now live longer.

items.name: Epidemiological transition (Omran)
items.pic: Stacked cause-of-death shares over two centuries move from infections toward chronic disease, with life expectancy plotted on top.

items.name: The sex gap in life expectancy
items.pic: Male and female e₀ over time by country; decompose the gap by age and cause to see the twentieth-century widening and recent narrowing tied to smoking.

items.name: The Function Expressive of the Law of Human Mortality

paper.title: On the Nature of the Function Expressive of the Law of Human Mortality, and on a New Mode of Determining the Value of Life Contingencies
paper.venue: Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London 115: 513–583

items.pic: Gompertz’s observation that the force of mortality grows geometrically with adult age: fit μ(x) = Bcˣ to the Northampton and Carlisle tables he worked from, read off the doubling time of the death rate (about eight years), and see where the straight line of log mortality bends away at the youngest and oldest ages.

items.name: Modeling and Forecasting U.S. Mortality

paper.authors: Ronald D. Lee and Lawrence R. Carter
paper.title: Modeling and Forecasting U.S. Mortality
paper.venue: Journal of the American Statistical Association 87 (419): 659–671

items.pic: US death rates by age, 1900–1989, decomposed as ln m(x, t) = aₓ + bₓkₜ by a singular value decomposition: the single mortality index kₜ falls almost linearly, so it is forecast as a random walk with drift; draw the fan of projected life expectancy (the paper’s central forecast reaches about 86 years by 2065) and compare it with the years observed since.

chapters.title: Fertility and reproduction
chapters.summary: Fertility is measured by age-specific rates, summed into the total fertility rate; folding in survival gives the net reproduction rate, which is exactly one at replacement. Period measures can mislead when people postpone childbearing, and a few proximate determinants — marriage, contraception, breastfeeding, abortion — account for most variation between societies. Sampling quirks also matter: children see larger families than mothers have.

items.name: Age-specific fertility rates
items.pic: Fertility schedules by age for several countries; drag the peak earlier or later and the area under each curve (the TFR) is reported.

items.name: Total fertility rate
items.pic: Sum the age-specific rates as bars stacked into one column; the column height is the number of children a woman would have at current rates.

items.name: Gross and net reproduction rates
refs: UN Demographic Yearbook, natality Table 3 technical notes: definitions, computation and limitations
UN World Population Prospects 2024, fertility by age5, female abridged life tables and demographic indicators
items.pic: Count live daughters at birth, weighting the prospective mother’s survival to childbearing. Exact band integrals of one reconstructed survival power determine the net bars; compare the official-L grouped reference and published UN NRR separately.

items.name: Replacement-level fertility
items.pic: Solve for the TFR that makes NRR = 1 as you change survival to childbearing ages; replacement is about 2.1 with low mortality and above 3 with high mortality.

items.name: Mean age at childbearing and generation length
items.pic: The centre of mass of the fertility schedule and of the net-maternity function are marked; shifting births later lengthens the generation and slows growth for the same NRR.

items.name: The tempo effect (Bongaarts–Feeney)
items.pic: Cohorts all have two children but postpone them by a month each year; the period TFR drops below two while postponement lasts, and the Bongaarts–Feeney adjustment recovers the true level.

items.name: Proximate determinants of fertility (Bongaarts)
items.pic: Start from a biological maximum of about fifteen births and apply multiplicative indices for marriage, contraception, postpartum infecundability and abortion; each slider’s effect on TFR is shown.

items.name: Natural versus controlled fertility (Coale–Trussell)
refs: UN Manual X (1983), chapter I.E.1, pp.23–25, Table3 and equations E.3–E.7
items.pic: Generate a hypothetical marital schedule with the official standard; fit its log ratio at ages20–44, and expose age-pattern departures and the excluded45–49 prediction.

items.name: Princeton fertility indices (I_f, I_g, I_m)
refs: Coale, Factors associated with the development of low fertility (1967), pp.205–209, especially Tables1–2
UN World Population Prospects 2024, fertility by age5: ASFR and births
items.pic: Use matched15–49 WPP period rates/exposures and the adjusted Hutterite reference. Authored current-marriage shares and nonmarital allocation illustrate the complete four-index identity without a unit cap.

items.name: Children come from larger families than women have
items.pic: A population of mothers with various family sizes; sample children instead of mothers and the average family size jumps to mean + variance/mean, Preston’s inspection-paradox result.

items.name: Human sex ratios from birth to old age
items.pic: About 105 boys are born per 100 girls; apply male and female life tables and the sex ratio by age falls through parity near reproductive ages to a large female majority among the old, as Fisher’s principle and excess male mortality suggest.

items.name: Sex ratio at birth and “missing women”
items.pic: Observed sex ratios at birth by birth order for several countries against the biological norm of about 105; the cumulative gap converts into an estimate of missing women.

chapters.title: Age structure and projection
chapters.summary: Explicit age-census accounting, fixed-matrix spectral limits and replacement momentum, with authored cohort echoes and clearly scoped finite uncertainty ensembles.

items.pic: Edit the full age vector and change the five-year-aligned work brackets. Colored age bars identify each numerator and denominator; the three ratio bars update. Empty working-age counts produce an explicit undefined state.

refs: Rodríguez, Population Projections (Princeton2017), pp1–3, female grouped-census coefficients
UN WPP2024 Methodology I.A and appendix B; accounting versus assumed components
items.pic: Step the actual female census forward, vary fertility, mortality and end-census immigration, and select a source cohort. The age bars show its carryover alongside the entire next census; a signed ledger checks all population flows.

refs: Rodríguez, Population Projections pp2–3, actual maternity row and Leslie organization
items.pic: Choose an output row and input census. The highlighted matrix row and contribution bars compute that exact next-bin count. Vary fertility and mortality to see the top row and survival subdiagonal change together.

refs: Yuan Yao, HKUST Lecture8, actual PDF p16 primitive Perron–Frobenius; p18 periodic example
Written Jordan form; independent spectral projection derivation
items.pic: Compare actual finite total-growth ratios with the computed spectral root. Switch between a human census law, a primitive full diagnostic, a periodic law, a sterile chain and a reducible reproductive core; select the census whose age vector is shown.

Yao Lecture8 PDF p18, fixed stochastic-matrix convergence only

refs: UNFPA, Demographic dividend, actual definition and conditional-investment discussion; no source economic example reproduced
Own explicitly conditional output accounting identity

refs: UN WPP2024 Methodology II.G printedp56, actual probabilistic-versus-deterministic workflow and uncertainty limits

chapters.title: Stable and stationary populations
chapters.summary: If age-specific rates stay fixed, any closed population settles into a stable state with constant growth rate r and a fixed age distribution — Lotka’s result, which lets demographers infer a population’s structure from its rates alone. A stable population’s age pyramid depends far more on fertility than on mortality. The stationary population (r = 0) links births, deaths and life expectancy by simple identities, and later work relaxed stability to variable rates.

items.name: The stable population model
items.pic: Under constant rates the projected pyramid stops changing shape and just scales; a toggle overlays the analytic stable distribution on the projected one.

items.name: Lotka’s intrinsic growth rate from a life table
items.pic: Plot ∫ e^{−ra} l(a) m(a) da against r for a real human schedule; the curve falls monotonically and crosses one at a unique r, read off live as you edit fertility.

items.name: r ≈ ln(NRR) / T for human populations
items.pic: Scatter the exact r against ln NRR / T for every country’s schedule; points hug the diagonal, and the error grows only for very high fertility.

items.name: The stable age distribution c(a) = b e^{−ra} l(a)
items.pic: Build the stable pyramid from a survival curve and r; raising r tilts the pyramid into a wide-based triangle, lowering it below zero inverts the top.

items.name: Fertility, not mortality, shapes the age pyramid (Coale)
items.pic: Change fertility and mortality separately in a stable population: lowering mortality barely changes the mean age (it saves the young as much as the old), while lowering fertility ages the population sharply.

items.name: Stationary-population identities: b = d = 1/e₀
items.pic: Set r = 0 and see the pyramid become the survival curve on its side; the crude birth and death rates both equal 1/e₀, and the mean age of the living matches its formula.

items.name: Lotka’s renewal equation and convergence to stability
items.pic: Births computed from the renewal equation oscillate in damped waves of generation length before settling on e^{rt}; the complex roots that govern the waves are plotted in the plane.

items.name: Variable-r relations (Preston–Coale)
items.pic: For a non-stable population, compute age-specific growth rates from two censuses; the generalized formula c(a) = b exp(−∫₀ᵃ r(x)dx) l(a) reproduces the observed age distribution exactly.

items.name: Weak ergodicity under changing rates
items.pic: Two different starting pyramids subjected to the same sequence of time-varying rates converge toward each other, though neither settles into a fixed shape.

items.name: The two-sex problem
items.pic: Male- and female-based projections of the same population disagree on r; a marriage-squeeze slider shows how a harmonic-mean pairing function reconciles them.

items.name: A Problem in Age-Distribution

paper.authors: F. R. Sharpe and Alfred J. Lotka
paper.title: A Problem in Age-Distribution

items.pic: Start a population from any age pyramid with fixed age-specific fertility and survival: births oscillate in dying waves while the age distribution converges to the stable shape c(a) = b e^(−ra) l(a), with r the real root of their characteristic equation; edit the starting pyramid to see that the destination does not depend on it.

items.name: How the Age Distribution of a Human Population Is Determined

paper.title: How the Age Distribution of a Human Population Is Determined
paper.venue: Cold Spring Harbor Symposia on Quantitative Biology 22: 83–89

items.pic: Two sliders, fertility and mortality, drive a stable population’s pyramid: raising fertility turns it from a column into a broad triangle, while lowering mortality, which mostly saves infants and children, barely changes its shape and can even make the population younger; compare the stable pyramids with observed ones from the 1950s.

chapters.title: Population and development
chapters.summary: Malthus argued that population growth would always be checked by misery as it outran food, which described the pre-industrial world reasonably well. The demographic transition — mortality falling first, fertility later — broke that trap, with an interlude of rapid growth that peaked in the 1960s. Why fertility fell (economics, mortality, ideas spreading) is still debated, and many countries now face very low fertility and ageing.

items.name: The Malthusian population trap
items.pic: Population and income per head with diminishing returns to land; a technology shock briefly raises income, then population grows until income returns to subsistence.

items.name: Preventive and positive checks
items.pic: English wages and vital rates, 1540–1800: marriage (the preventive check) and deaths (the positive check) respond to real wages with lags drawn on linked plots.

items.name: Boserup: population pressure drives innovation
items.pic: Toggle the Malthusian and Boserupian feedback in one model: denser populations either starve or intensify agriculture, producing very different long-run paths.

items.name: The demographic transition
items.pic: Birth and death rates for England, Sweden, India and Nigeria aligned by stage; the gap between the curves (natural increase) is shaded and its timing compared across countries.

items.name: European fertility decline: economics or diffusion?
items.pic: Map the date of a 10% fall in marital fertility across European provinces; colouring by language or by income shows declines clustering by culture more than by economic level.

items.name: The second demographic transition (contested)
items.pic: Cohabitation, non-marital births and below-replacement fertility across countries since 1970, with the values-shift and economic explanations offered as alternative overlays.

items.name: Very low fertility and population decline
items.pic: Project South Korea at TFR 0.8: each generation is about 60% smaller than the last, and negative momentum keeps the population shrinking even if fertility recovers.

items.name: Population ageing
items.pic: Median age and old-age dependency projected to 2100 for world regions; separate the contributions of low fertility and longer lives with two sliders.

items.name: Easterlin’s relative-cohort-size hypothesis
items.pic: A feedback model in which small cohorts earn more and have more children: the simulated births oscillate with a two-generation cycle, compared with U.S. births after the baby boom.

items.name: World population growth peaked in the 1960s
items.pic: World population and its annual growth rate since 1700 on twin axes: the growth rate peaked near 2.1% around 1968 and has roughly halved, while absolute numbers keep rising.

items.name: An Essay on the Principle of Population

paper.title: An Essay on the Principle of Population, as It Affects the Future Improvement of Society

items.pic: Malthus’s two ratios: population doubling every 25 years (1, 2, 4, 8, 16, …) against subsistence growing by equal additions (1, 2, 3, 4, 5, …); watch the gap open, then switch on the preventive check (later marriage, fewer births) or the positive check (misery and higher deaths) and see population pinned to the food supply, with income per head held near subsistence.

chapters.title: Kinship, migration and multistate models
chapters.summary: Rates determine not only population size but family structure: from fertility and mortality alone one can compute how many sisters, cousins or living grandparents a typical person has. Migration follows strong age patterns and distance decay. Multistate life tables generalize the single exit of death to movements among states — regions, marital status, health — modelled as a Markov chain on the life course.

items.name: Kinship from rates (Goodman–Keyfitz–Pullum)
refs: K&C: The Demographic Theory of Kinship
items.pic: Choose a fertility and mortality regime; the expected numbers of living mothers, sisters, daughters and cousins at each age are computed and drawn as a family tree with fractional people.

items.name: Low-fertility kinship: fewer cousins, more grandparents
refs: K&C: The Demographic Theory of Kinship
items.pic: Slide from a 1900 to a 2020 regime: the family tree thins sideways (siblings, cousins) and lengthens vertically (living grandparents), the “beanpole family”.

items.name: Gravity model and Ravenstein’s laws of migration
items.pic: Flows between cities scale with the product of populations over a power of distance; fit the exponent to internal migration data and map the predicted and observed flows.

items.name: Rogers–Castro model migration schedule
items.pic: Migration rates by age have a childhood component, a labour-force peak near age 23 and a retirement bump; drag each component’s parameters to fit an observed schedule.

items.name: Increment–decrement (multistate) life tables
items.pic: A cohort flowing among married, single and dead states with transition rates you set; the expected years spent in each state appear as coloured areas under the survival curve.

items.name: Markov chains for individual life histories
refs: K&C: Markov Chains for Individual Life Histories
items.pic: The same multistate table as a transition matrix; simulated individual paths and the fundamental matrix give the mean and variance of time spent in each state.

items.name: Replacement migration
items.pic: How many immigrants per year would keep a country’s population, workforce or support ratio constant? Three required-migration curves are computed, the last one implausibly large.
